title: Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes
description: Brute force to optimized: DFS over every walk order directly versus a multi-source BFS over (node, bitmask) states.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given an undirected, connected graph of n nodes (n at most 12) as an adjacency list, return the length of the shortest possible walk (edges traversed, revisiting nodes and edges is allowed) that visits every node at least once, starting from any node.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","graph as an adjacency list"],["Output","Shortest walk length (edge count) visiting every node at least once"],["Key Insight","Since n is at most 12, the SET of nodes visited so far can be represented as a bitmask, turning the state space into (current node, bitmask)"],["Constraints","n <= 12, graph is connected"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Visit every node, small n (at most 12)\"","A classic bitmask DP / BFS-over-states signal: the small n allows representing \"which nodes have been visited\" as a single integer bitmask"],["\"Shortest walk length\"","BFS over an expanded state space (current node, visited bitmask) finds the shortest number of steps to reach ANY state with the full bitmask"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Since revisiting nodes is allowed, this is NOT a simple shortest Hamiltonian path problem; instead, think of it as a BFS not just over individual nodes, but over PAIRS (current node, set of nodes visited so far). Since n is at most 12, this visited set fits neatly into a bitmask (an integer with n bits). A standard multi-source BFS over this expanded state space (starting simultaneously from every single node, each with only itself marked visited) finds the shortest number of steps to reach ANY state where the bitmask has all n bits set.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Delivery Route That May Backtrack, Tracked by Location Plus a Checklist
blocks.text: Picture a delivery driver who may revisit streets, needing to visit every neighborhood at least once, tracked not just by CURRENT location but by a checklist of neighborhoods already visited. Exploring level by level (BFS) over (location, checklist) pairs, starting from every possible starting location simultaneously, finds the fewest steps needed for the checklist to become fully complete.

blocks.caption: Represent the visited set as a bitmask; BFS over (current node, bitmask) state pairs

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: graph = [[1,2,3],[0],[0],[0]] (a star graph, node 0 connected to 1, 2, 3)
Result: 4 (a walk like 1-0-2-0-3 visits all four nodes in 4 edges).
Result: 4.
5. How Should We Think?

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since revisiting nodes is allowed, the problem is really about the fewest STEPS to reach a point where every node has been touched at least once, not about finding a simple path.

Observation 2: Representing "which nodes have been visited so far" as a bitmask (since n is at most 12, fitting comfortably in an integer) allows the SAME (node, visited-set) combination to be recognized and never reprocessed, avoiding infinite revisiting loops.

Observation 3: Starting a BFS SIMULTANEOUSLY from every node (each starting with only itself marked visited in its bitmask) correctly considers every possible starting point without needing n separate BFS runs.

Observation 4: The BFS explores neighbors normally, but each move updates the CURRENT node and OR's the destination bit into the current bitmask; the first time any state's bitmask becomes the FULL mask (all n bits set), that state's BFS depth is the answer, since BFS guarantees the first time a state is reached is via the shortest possible number of steps.
This leads to a multi-source BFS over (node, bitmask) states, returning the depth at which any state first reaches the full bitmask.
6. Brute Force Solution

Recursively (via DFS/backtracking) try every possible walk order directly, tracking the set of visited nodes as the walk extends, without recognizing and reusing already-explored (node, visited-set) states.

codes.python:
# Conceptually: recursively try extending a walk one node at a time from
# the current node, tracking the growing set of visited nodes, and
# recording the walk length whenever all nodes become visited, taking the
# minimum over every possible starting node and walk order. Correct, but
# without recognizing that many different walks can reach the exact SAME
# (current node, visited set) combination, this revisits the same states
# repeatedly, an exponential blow-up.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every walk order directly via DFS implements the definition literally.

This revisits the SAME (node, visited set) combination via many different walk orders repeatedly, without ever recognizing this redundancy, costing exponential time; treating (node, bitmask) as a single BFS state avoids ever re-exploring the same combination twice.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential, revisiting the same (node, visited set) combinations across many different walk orders.
Space: O(walk length) recursion depth.
Limitation: BFS over (node, bitmask) states, marking each combination visited exactly once, guarantees every distinct state is explored at most once, in increasing order of walk length.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Initialize a BFS queue with EVERY node as a starting state: (node i, bitmask with only bit i set, distance 0), marking each as visited immediately. Process the queue in standard BFS order: for the current (node, mask, dist), if mask already equals the full bitmask (all n bits set), return dist immediately (BFS guarantees this is the shortest such distance). Otherwise, for every neighbor of the current node, compute the new bitmask (OR-ing in the neighbor's bit); if this exact (neighbor, new mask) combination has not been visited before, mark it visited and enqueue it with distance dist+1.
Use a multi-source BFS over (node, bitmask) states, returning the depth at which any state first reaches the full bitmask.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run intuition for the star graph [[1,2,3],[0],[0],[0]]

blocks.content: {"headers":["BFS depth","Example state reached"],"rows":[["0","starting at node 1, mask={1} (bit 1 set)"],["1","move to node 0, mask={0,1}"],["2","move to node 2, mask={0,1,2}"],["3","move to node 0, mask still {0,1,2}"],["4","move to node 3, mask={0,1,2,3}, the FULL mask, answer is 4"]]}

blocks.text: Why This Works

Treating (current node, visited bitmask) as a single unified BFS state correctly captures everything relevant to future decisions (revisiting the SAME combination via a longer path can never help, since BFS already reaches it via the shortest possible route the first time); starting simultaneously from every node correctly considers every possible starting point without redundant separate BFS runs, and the first time any state's bitmask becomes the full mask, BFS guarantees that depth is the minimum possible walk length.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared times 2 raised to n), the total number of (node, bitmask) states times edges per node.
Space: O(n times 2 raised to n) for the visited set and queue.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["DFS over every walk order directly","Exponential, with massive redundant re-exploration","O(walk length) recursion depth","Correct, but far too slow."],["BFS over (node, bitmask) states","O(n squared times 2^n)","O(n times 2^n)","The expected, efficient solution given the small n <= 12 constraint."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes is a classic bitmask-state BFS problem: the small n (at most 12) is the tell that a visited-set bitmask should become part of the search state itself.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to start the BFS simultaneously from EVERY node (a multi-source BFS), instead running n separate BFS searches unnecessarily.
Not recognizing (node, bitmask) as a SINGLE combined state, causing the same combination to be explored repeatedly via different walk histories.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single node graph (n=1)","The answer is 0, already fully \"visited\" with no edges needed."],["A graph where one node connects to all others (a star)","The optimal walk alternates back through the central node."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "the small n signals a bitmask should be part of the search state" is the key recognition that unlocks this entire class of problems.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "visit every node, small n (at most around 20)", think: bitmask represents the visited set, becoming part of the BFS or DP state itself.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you adapt this to a WEIGHTED graph, where edges have varying costs (using Dijkstra over the same expanded state space instead of plain BFS)?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Traveling Salesman Problem (bitmask DP) and Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets, other classic small-n bitmask-state problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The naive DFS-over-every-walk-order approach is exponential with massive redundant re-exploration; the bitmask-state BFS costs O(n squared times 2^n), the standard efficient solution for this constraint size.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: multi-source BFS over an expanded (node, visited-bitmask) state space.
Core Idea: the small n (at most 12) allows the visited set to be represented as a bitmask, becoming part of the search state to avoid redundant re-exploration.
Time: exponential with redundant re-exploration for the naive DFS, O(n squared times 2^n) for the bitmask BFS.
Space: O(walk length) recursion depth for the naive DFS, O(n times 2^n) for the bitmask BFS.
Most Important Observation: (current node, visited bitmask) together form a single, reusable BFS state.
Interview Difficulty: a hard bitmask-state search problem, a very recognizable pattern once spotted.
One line memory trick: bitmask the visited set, then BFS over (node, mask) pairs.
